Neonatal Greater sirens (Siren lacertina) emerge from their gelatinous egg masses following a period of embryonic development that concludes with eclosion, at which point the free-swimming larvae measure approximately 1.6 cm [Lb = approximately 1.6 cm] in total length. This modest size at birth, corresponding to a snout–vent length of about 1.3 cm, places them among the smaller-bodied amphibian larvae at the onset of exogenous feeding, a stage when the young must begin actively capturing microinvertebrates to sustain rapid growth. Field studies conducted in the sluggish, heavily vegetated waterways of the southeastern United States indicate that these newly hatched individuals initially rely on their remaining yolk reserves for a short period before transitioning to active foraging. The protracted egg incubation and subsequent larval period, which collectively span roughly 60 days [ab = roughly 60 days] under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], reflect a developmental strategy attuned to the relatively stable thermal environment of subtropical aquatic habitats. This duration from fertilisation to hatching, while not exceptionally long compared to some other paedomorphic salamanders, underscores the species’ reliance on warm, consistent water temperatures to drive embryogenesis efficiently.

As the larval Siren lacertina progresses through its extended aquatic tadpole stage, growth is comparatively slow and gradual, a pattern that contrasts sharply with many anuran and urodele species that undergo rapid metamorphosis within a single season. Juveniles remain fully aquatic and gill-bearing throughout their development, maintaining a permanently paedomorphic morphology. The species does not undergo a dramatic larval–juvenile transition involving tail resorption or limb emergence; instead, the body plan remains largely unchanged from the late larval phase through to adulthood. By the time individuals reach the size threshold associated with gonadal maturation, they typically measure between 22 and 25 cm in total length (22–25 cm) [Lp = 22–25 cm], with the most frequently cited value for the total length at puberty being 23.5 cm [Lp = 23.5 cm]. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, derived from the allometric relationship linking body length to mass, is approximately 14.2 grams [Wwp = approximately 14.2 grams], a value consistent with the relatively slender, elongated body form of this species compared to more robust-bodied amphibians of similar length. This pubertal transition occurs after a sustained period of somatic investment in the warm, resource-rich waters of lentic and slow-flowing lotic systems, where prey availability is high throughout much of the year.

Reproductive output in the Greater siren is notable for its magnitude, particularly given the species’ fully aquatic, paedomorphic life history. Gravid females produce large numbers of small, yolky eggs that are deposited in gelatinous clusters attached to submerged vegetation or debris. Based on counts from field-collected clutches and dissections of gravid individuals, each female typically deposits several hundred eggs per clutch [N_R_i = several hundred eggs per clutch], with an estimated clutch frequency of approximately 3.8 clutches annually [F_R_i = approximately 3.8 clutches annually] under stable, warm-water conditions, such as those encountered in the species’ native range at a water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This combination of high per-clutch fecundity and relatively frequent annual reproduction yields a cumulative annual output that is among the highest recorded for any salamander. The sustained production of clutches over an extended reproductive period likely compensates for the high rates of egg and larval mortality typical of lentic environments with abundant predatory fish and macroinvertebrates.

The ultimate size attained by Siren lacertina is impressive among members of the Sirenidae, with the largest confirmed individuals reaching a total length of 97 cm [Li = 97 cm], a dimension that places this species among the longest salamanders in the world. Corresponding to this extreme linear dimension, the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is approximately 1000 grams [Wwi = approximately 1000 grams], a mass that reflects the animal’s elongated, serpentine body form rather than robust girth. Achieving this size requires an extended period of somatic growth that is closely tied to thermal regime; available data indicate that at a constant water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the total lifespan of this species reaches roughly 25 years [am = roughly 25 years]. Such longevity is exceptional among salamanders and is characteristic of a life-history strategy that prioritises slow, continuous growth, delayed reproduction, and high adult survivorship in relatively stable, predator-scarce aquatic refugia. The combination of extreme size and extended lifespan suggests that Greater sirens occupy a demographic niche in which individuals invest heavily in maintenance and somatic persistence, amortising reproductive effort across many decades rather than concentrating it into a brief adult stage.

Sexual maturation in Siren lacertina, defined as the attainment of functional gonads capable of gamete production, does not occur quickly despite the warm, productive environment these animals inhabit. Puberty is reached approximately 2 years after birth [tp = approximately 2 years after birth] when individuals are maintained under laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], a timeframe that represents a moderate delay relative to the few months required by many smaller-bodied amphibian species. This two-year period leading to reproductive competence allows the individual to accumulate sufficient body size—specifically, the 22 to 25 cm total length range characteristic of first reproduction—and to develop the energetic reserves necessary to support the substantial investment in repeated clutch production over an extended breeding season.
